sections.title: The Conversion of Minors
sections.html:
The beit din can convert minors, and therefore, when parents come to convert and ask to convert their children with them, the beit din converts their children. And although conversion depends on the decision of the convert, and children who have not yet reached the age of mitzvot do not have a mature mind to make such a fateful decision, since it is for the child's good to be of the same religion as his parents, who are responsible for him and take care of him, the beit din converts the minor on the authority of his parents (Ketubot 11a; SA YD 268:7).

The beit din can convert a minor even when the parents do not wish to convert themselves but wish the beit din to convert their child, or when the child decided on his own initiative that he wants to convert and his parents come before the beit din to express their consent to this. For since accepting Judaism is, as a rule, a good thing and a benefit (zekhut) for the child, if the beit din assesses that the conversion will indeed be a benefit for him, it will convert him on the authority of the beit din. For just as "one may confer a benefit on a person in his absence," and accordingly one may transfer gifts to a minor and confer upon him things that will be good for him, so the beit din may bring the minor into the covenant with God when in its assessment this is for the minor's good.

Similarly, in times and places in which there were abandoned children, if such a child came and asked to convert, the beit din can convert him. Likewise, when Jews want to adopt an abandoned infant and ask to convert him, since it is a privilege to be a Jew, and it is also for the infant's good to be a Jew like his adoptive parents, the beit din may accede to their request and convert the child (Shevet Mi-Yehuda vol. 2 YD 29; Mishpetei Shaul 1, Sha'ar 4, 38).

However, the beit din should not seek out children in order to convert them, and all the more so one should not convert children against their will. And even where Israel rules, one does not forcibly convert non-Jewish children against their will or against the will of their parents. And if they converted a child against his will, his conversion is void (Baḥ and Shakh 268:16).1

In the case of a child of a mixed marriage, when the Jewish father wants to convert his child and the non-Jewish mother opposes it, many say that one listens to the mother, for since the child is a non-Jew, according to halakha the father is not considered his father. And some say that the father too has authority to bring him, but if the mother opposes his conversion, it is often preferable not to convert him, because as a result of her opposition to his conversion, she will insist on educating him to hate Judaism.2

sections.title: Annulment of the Conversion by Protest
sections.html:
Since the minor's conversion takes place on the authority of the beit din, without the minor having an independent mind to convert, the Sages said that his conversion depends on his not protesting against the conversion when he grows up and has an independent mind. But if, when he grows up and reaches the age of mitzvot – twelve for a girl and thirteen for a boy – he protests against the conversion, the conversion is annulled. The simple way to protest against the conversion is for the minor to announce, even before he reaches the age of mitzvot, that he does not want to be a Jew; and if he remains of this mind until he reaches the age of mitzvot, his conversion is annulled.

But if, after he reached the age of mitzvot, he began to fulfill mitzvot as a Jew, the conversion has been confirmed and completed, and it can never again be annulled. And even if that child did not receive a religious education, and his parents habitually desecrate Shabbat, as long as upon reaching the age of mitzvot he wanted to be a Jew and fulfilled even just one mitzva as a Jew – for example, he put on tefillin, or was called up to the Torah, or participated in the Shabbat Kiddush – he thereby confirmed the conversion, and can never again annul it.

One whose parents converted him when he was a minor, and afterward they distanced themselves from Judaism and raised him as a non-Jew, until he did not know at all that he had been converted as a minor: even though in practice he fulfilled many mitzvot between a person and his fellow, and perhaps even adopted Jewish customs, since he did not know that he had been converted, and did not do the mitzvot as a Jew, his status remains in suspense. Only after he knows that they converted him, and they inform him of some of the mitzvot, their reward and their punishment, can he protest or confirm his conversion.

One who grew up in a religious family and did not know that he had been converted in his childhood, and many years after he grew up observing mitzvot learned that he had been converted in his childhood – according to many, he can protest and decide to renounce his conversion (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ketubot 1:35). For the mitzvot that he fulfilled did not testify to his consent to the conversion, since he did not know that he had been converted as a minor. Therefore, it is good to tell the child that he is a convert before he reaches the age of mitzvot, and by fulfilling one mitzva after he grows up, he will confirm his conversion and will never again be able to annul it.3

Many say that a minor convert can annul his conversion by protest only when he converted alone, without his parents, for then his conversion is on the authority of the beit din; but if he converted with his parents, he can never protest. For since they are his parents, they accept the terms of the conversion on his behalf, just as Israel at the Sinai assembly entered into the covenant with God together with their young children, without the children being able to protest (Responsa Ḥatam Sofer YD 253). And some do not accept this distinction, and hold that a minor convert can always protest when he grows up, and so it is implied from the view of most Rishonim.4

sections.title: The Procedure of a Minor's Conversion and His Status
sections.html:
When the minor is immersed for conversion, one of the members of the beit din recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the immersion of converts." And if one of his parents enters the water with him to immerse him, the parent may recite the blessing on behalf of the beit din. If the child is older and understands and wants to recite the blessing himself, in order to include him in the mitzva, one may rely on those who hold that the child can recite the blessing.5 When the child is male, they perform a brit mila for him with the blessings, as is done for an adult convert.

According to most poskim, the validity of a minor's conversion is from the Torah. And although a minor's conversion is not final, for if he protests when he grows up the conversion will be annulled, as long as he has not protested his conversion is treated as a definite conversion. Therefore one recites blessings over his circumcision and his immersion. And if he slaughters an animal properly, since he is a Jew his slaughter is kosher, and we are not concerned that perhaps after he reaches the age of mitzvot he will protest and annul his conversion, and it will turn out that his slaughter was invalid. For since he was educated as a Jew, there is a presumption that he will not protest (Rashba and Ritva on Ketubot 11a).6

sections.title: Those Who Are Stringent Regarding the Conversion of a Minor Who Will Not Be Educated in Mitzvot
sections.html:
As we learned (above 6:4-6), the poskim disagreed whether to convert spouses of Jews who do not intend to fulfill mitzvot as people with a religious way of life, but rather as secular people with a "Jewish identity." The stringent hold that one should not convert one who does not intend to maintain a religious way of life, and some of them even hold that such a conversion is void. In contrast, the lenient hold that in a pressing situation, in order to save the Jew from assimilation, it is proper to convert the non-Jewish spouse when he intends to fulfill mitzvot in the manner of people with a "Jewish identity." And likewise it is proper to convert descendants of Jews so that they will not assimilate among the nations and be lost to Israel.

Similarly, the poskim disagreed whether the beit din may, or even must, convert a child of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother, or a non-Jewish infant whom a Jewish couple want to adopt, when the parents do not maintain a religious way of life. According to the stringent, only when the parents intend to educate the minor to maintain a religious way of life is it possible to convert him. And according to the lenient, it is possible to convert him even when they intend to educate him to fulfill mitzvot like people with a "Jewish identity." As a rule, the dispute concerning the conversion of minors corresponds to the dispute concerning the conversion of adults; however, since regarding a minor's conversion several considerations in both directions are added, some of those who are stringent about the conversion of adults were lenient about minors, and some of those who are lenient about the conversion of adults were stringent about minors.

According to the stringent, in the conversion of a minor two further considerations for stringency are added. The first: an ordinary conversion is done on the responsibility of the person converting, and if the person converting decided to convert even though he does not intend to maintain a religious way of life, the responsibility for this rests upon him, and the beit din is not obligated to prevent it from him when there is benefit in the conversion for preventing assimilation. But when it concerns a minor, the conversion is done by the beit din and on its responsibility, and therefore it is forbidden for it to convert one who is not expected to maintain a religious way of life, since thereby it causes him to be a sinner. For as long as he remains a non-Jew he is not obligated in the mitzvot, but if they convert him he will become obligated in all the mitzvot, and will be punished by Heaven for every Shabbat that he desecrates and for every forbidden food that he eats, as well as for all the transgressions that he commits. According to this consideration, one should not convert a minor who will not receive a religious education, but if they converted him, his conversion is valid.

The second consideration for stringency: since a minor's conversion is done by the beit din and as the minor's agent, the beit din has authority to convert him only when it is clear that the conversion is a benefit for the minor; but when it is a detriment (ḥova) for him, the beit din has no authority to convert him. According to this consideration, there is room to say that if the beit din accepted a minor whose parents do not intend to give him a religious education, his conversion is void.

Because of these two considerations, among the poskim who were lenient to convert adults who do not intend to maintain a religious way of life, some were stringent regarding minors who are not going to receive a religious education, and ruled not to convert them on the authority of the beit din but to wait until they grow up and decide on their own to convert.7

sections.title: Those Who Are Lenient Regarding the Conversion of a Minor Who Will Not Be Educated in Mitzvot
sections.html:
As a rule, those who are lenient to convert the non-Jewish spouse in order to prevent assimilation were also lenient to convert children of a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman who will not receive a religious education, in order to keep the Jew's descendants within the community of Israel. As Rav Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer wrote, that although the child's lineage follows only his non-Jewish mother, "nevertheless we find that he is called 'holy seed,' for when Ezra rebuked Israel who had married foreign women … he said (Ezra 9:2): 'and the holy seed has mingled with the peoples of the lands.'" Therefore one should make every possible effort that the seed of Israel not be lost among the nations but remain within the community of Israel. And this is also the view of many poskim.8
To the claim that the conversion is not a benefit for minors but a detriment, they replied that even being a Jew who does not maintain a religious way of life is a great privilege. As the Sages said (Ḥagiga 27a): "The fire of Gehinnom has no power over the transgressors of Israel," and so the Sages expounded (Yoma 56b): "'Who dwells with them in the midst of their impurities' (Vayikra 16:16) – even when they are impure, the Shekhina is with them." Likewise, in the future to come the converts too will receive an inheritance in the Land of Israel (Yeḥezkel 47:21-23, and commentators there; Kohelet Rabba 1:6).

And even Rav Yitzḥak Schmelkes, the founder of the approach of the stringent regarding the conversion of adults, was lenient in the conversion of minors. This is because in his view the conversion of adults depends on their sincere commitment to maintain a religious way of life, and one who did not sincerely commit to this – his conversion is void (Beit Yitzḥak YD 2:100). But regarding the conversion of minors he was lenient, because a minor's conversion depends on the authority of the beit din, and since even for one who does not observe mitzvot it is a privilege to be a Jew, the beit din can convert him even though his father is a secular Jew and his mother a non-Jew (there, EH 1:29:8). And Rav Feinstein inclined to this, that the conversion is a benefit for the minor even if he will not observe mitzvot (Igrot Moshe YD 1:158). And he ruled in practice to convert children of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother who study in a religious school, many of whose students were from non-religious families (Igrot Moshe EH 4:26).9

sections.title: Those Who Are Stringent Not to Circumcise the Son of a Jewish Man and a Non-Jewish Woman
sections.html:
Following the mixed marriages of recent generations, a question arose concerning Jews who married non-Jewish women who did not want to convert, and also did not want their children to convert, but agreed to accede to their partner's request to circumcise their son, according to his custom as a Jew.

Some rabbis were stringent and ruled not to circumcise their sons. First, because some say that it is forbidden to circumcise a non-Jew, because one should not grant the seal of the holy covenant of Israel to a non-Jew. And since the child is a non-Jew, it is forbidden to circumcise him outside the framework of a conversion process.

And even according to those who hold that it is permitted to circumcise a non-Jew, here it should be forbidden, because if they circumcise him, people may mistakenly think that he is a Jew, and a serious mishap may result from this, that a Jewish woman will think that he is a Jew and marry him, while in truth he is a non-Jew.

They raised another serious concern: perhaps agreeing to circumcise the sons of Jews who sinned by marrying a non-Jewish woman will reduce the severity of their sin and grant them a kind of after-the-fact consent to mixed marriage. And perhaps as a result, young people who are hesitating whether to cross the line and marry a non-Jewish woman will receive encouragement to do so.10

sections.title: Those Who Are Lenient to Circumcise the Son of a Jewish Man and a Non-Jewish Woman
sections.html:
In contrast, many poskim hold that one may accede to the father and circumcise his son, but since there is no intention now to continue with his conversion, one does not recite a blessing over his circumcision.

In their view, it is permitted to circumcise him because the halakha follows the majority of poskim, that it is permitted to circumcise a non-Jew for payment. In addition, the halakha follows the Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 268:9), that it is permitted to circumcise a non-Jew for the sake of a mitzva even though he does not intend to convert, since every non-Jew who circumcises himself thereby fulfills a mitzva. And regarding the concern of the stringent, that perhaps following the circumcision people will mistakenly think that he converted, they replied that one should not invent concerns that were not mentioned in the Talmud and the Rishonim (Rav Zirelsohn, Ma'arkhei Lev 55).

Those who permit were not concerned that agreeing to circumcise the sons would encourage mixed marriages, since they knew that refusing to circumcise the children, like refusing to convert the non-Jewish partners, would in the vast majority of cases not prevent the mixed marriages. On the contrary, by agreeing to circumcise the sons, there is a chance that later on they will want to convert and to be of their father's religion. As Rav Kalischer wrote, there is a mitzva in this, for by circumcising him while he is still a minor, one opens a wide door for him to enable his conversion when he grows up, and thereby one saves the seed of Israel from being lost among the nations. For if they do not circumcise him, there is a concern that even if he wants to convert when he grows up, he will be deterred by the pain of circumcision, whereas now that he is already circumcised, he will be able to decide on it easily.

In practice, many of those who permit circumcising the sons made it conditional on the non-Jewish mother agreeing to it (Maharam Schick YD 248; Maharsham 3:360). Apparently they were concerned that if the circumcision were done against the mother's will, she would rise up against Judaism, and thus the chance that the son would draw close to Judaism and convert would diminish.11
